A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on." `render_text` prints id, proposition, optional pin, and "scope: WITHHELD" per item; `render_json` the same fields.

src/checks.rs lines 630-760, `analyze_ledger(claims, evidence)`. Per claim it filters `evidence` by `claim_id`, computes `current = crate::evidence::sha256_hex(&claim.proposition)` — proposition text alone — and partitions records with a NON-EMPTY `proposition_digest` into `fresh` (digest == current) and `stale`. A stale record goes to `out_of_proof` when `fresh.is_empty()`, else to `superseded` (never a failure, log is append-only). `ungrounded` is pushed only when `records.is_empty()` — i.e. no evidence record at all for the id, regardless of digest. A separate set `grading_current` = records whose digest is empty OR equals current; the comment says a record with no digest predates the field and is "treated as grading the current text rather than dropped", grandfathered because that direction "fails loudly".

## ## The anchor: first proof, not last pass

The ticket's phrase "the last grounding pass" is not merely ambiguous, as its own open questions suspected — read literally it is self-defeating, and this is the design's first and largest departure. Every grounding pass is briefed on every claim in the ledger, whether or not it has been graded before, so a pass that finds nothing to change still appends a fresh record against the unchanged wording. The two memos already in this tree show what that produces: one claim carrying ten records on a single unchanged digest, written by three passes across nearly half an hour, and another graded `qualifies` twice by different passes a quarter of an hour apart on text nobody touched. Anchor the comparison at the most recent grading and the anchor walks forward every round; fix-round prose written in round three stops being "since the last pass" the moment round four runs, even though no pass has ever read a word of the prose. On the ticket's own account of it, the trail this residue is named after ran six rounds. So the anchor is the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof. A later pass over unchanged text cannot move it, and only a revision of the claim itself, followed by a grading of the new wording, ever does.

*cites: C3*

## ## The rule

With the anchor fixed, the rule almost states itself, and the places where it does not are the places attack put there. A prose block is listed when it is a paragraph rather than a heading, it cites at least one id, at least one cited id resolves to a ledger claim that is in proof, and the block's text timestamp is later than the latest first proof among those in-proof citations. "In proof" is not a new predicate: it is the digest comparison `analyze_ledger` already performs, empty-digest grandfathering included. The block's text timestamp is the earliest event in its history whose text and citation list both equal the current ones. Neither half of that definition was in the first draft of this design and neither is decoration — the next two sections are about what each one closes. The two quantifier choices the ticket left open fall out of the anchor rather than being decided by taste. Per claim, take the earliest in-proof record, because that is when the wording settled. Per block, take the latest of those, because a block is not anchored until its evidence base has settled — taking the earliest instead would list every paragraph whose text merely postdates its first-graded citation, which is nearly all of them. Both memos already in this tree list nothing, and that includes the two real post-pass prose revisions they contain between them, tet29's P4 and tet28's P18. Each was rewritten in a fix round after a pass had run, and each is correctly silent for the same reason: each also cites a claim revised in that same round, whose new wording entered proof only afterwards. The maximum is doing exactly the work it was chosen for. That also means the listing behaviour had to be tested on constructions appended to those logs rather than on a real defect: move a tet29 paragraph past its claim's first proof and touch no claim, and it is listed alone.

*cites: C4*

On the ticket's first open question — creation or revision — the residue is about neither act specifically but about the text's age: the timestamp is derived from the block's events without caring whether the earliest one bearing its current wording was a creation or a rewrite. The exposure is the same in both directions, since a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one, and the ticket's own vector could have arrived either way. Counting creations also cannot inflate the list through paragraphs added to carry a new assertion under a new claim, and the reason is mechanical rather than statistical: a claim not yet in proof cannot anchor a block at all, and once a pass has put it in proof that first proof necessarily postdates a paragraph written before the pass ran. How often a fix-round paragraph takes that shape rather than resting on old claims is a question about how authors behave, and nothing here measures it. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, settled claims.

## No opt-out, and what "explicitly named" costs

There should be no `--include-tetel`. The honest escape hatch already exists three times over, and each time it is reached by naming something rather than by setting a flag: open the file with `look <path>`, search with a tetel path as the root, or use `run`. The second of those is not a concession this design makes but a constraint it is under, since grep suppresses a directory named as the recursion root when `--exclude-dir` matches it, so the flags have to be withheld there or naming a snapshot directory would return nothing at all. The third is the hole the ticket already states and cannot be closed: `run` spawns its argv directly with nothing between the empty-argument refusal and the spawn that inspects the command or the paths it will touch, so there is no place an exclusion could be applied even in principle. A flag would add a fourth route with a property none of these has — it leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call.

*cites: C16*

The hard case the ticket asked about is a root like `docs/design`, which in this repository contains nine entries and not one of them is anything but tetel's own output. Under this rule it is not explicitly named — it is an ordinary directory whose path says nothing about tetel — so the exclusions apply and a search rooted there returns nothing at all where today it returns 1,200,881 bytes. That is a real loss and it is accepted deliberately, because the alternative is to decide that a directory counts as named when everything under it happens to be tetel's, which is a judgement about contents rather than a test on a path, and this project does not let a refusal make judgements. The price is one extra keystroke of specificity: to search across memos, name a memo or a snapshot, not the folder they live in.


Stop when `check` is machine-clean and no live claim is refuted or unexplained. Report then.

**Human-owed items never clear and are not failures.** `check` will always list qualified verdicts,
`proc:` extents, self-grounding, and its own standing non-coverage. Machine-checked clean is the
bar; the human-owed partition is what you hand the reader, not a queue to empty. Surviving
qualifications belong in your report with the grounder's own words.

**Stop after the first round that provokes no revision. Do not run a second.** Measured across all
four memos: the final grading pass provoked **zero** claim revisions every time. So the last round is
never free — it is what tells you the design has settled, and it is worth paying once. One memo paid
twice: two consecutive dry rounds, 55 records between them, nothing changed by either. The second was
waste under any stop rule. A round that changes nothing has done its job; a second one has not. This
is the floor; the cap below is the ceiling, and a run should hit whichever comes first.

**Cap yourself at four grounding rounds.** If you are still not clean, stop and say so plainly:
which claims will not survive, what each pass said, and what you believe the design cannot currently
establish. An honest report of an unstable design is a result. A design reported as finished because
the loop ran out of patience is not — and it is worse than the unstable one, because it arrives with
a green attached.

note:
Two observations on the pin operands.

(1) src/facts.rs lines 400-455: a fact's `pin` is `format!("sha256:{}", sha256_hex(&hash_input))` where hash_input concatenates, for every pending entry, its label, world_root, world_state and output. The comment calls it "a content fingerprint over every entry's label, output and world-tree marker", folding the marker in so "a fact minted against a different tree state pins differently even if its labels/output happen to coincide" — and notes the marker "is still carried separately in `extent`". So a fact pin is a hash of the observation's content, not a tree identifier: two facts minted in one checkout at one commit pin differently whenever their labels or output differ.

(2) Running the installed tetel binary as `brief --json` over all five rendered memos in docs/design (tet28, tet29, tet30, tet46, tet47): 15, 14, 13, 19 and 26 claims respectively — 87 in total — and ZERO carry a `pin` in any of them. `render_json` omits the field when `Claim::pin` is None, so `find_stated_pin` yields None for every claim in every memo this project has written, including this one.

Two observations on where a tree state is and is not available.

(1) src/evidence.rs lines 548-600, the record read-back. `EvidenceRecord` is constructed from the statement with claim_id, verdict, pass, reported_kind, source, extent, note, pin, timestamp, witnessed and proposition_digest — the predicate's `world: Vec<Marker>` field is NOT read back. So the tree markers a witnessed record carries are written into the evidence JSONL and dropped when it is loaded for `check`.

(2) src/lib.rs lines 130-150: when a snapshot directory sits beside the memo, `check` loads the shipped `facts.jsonl` via `facts::load_all(&snapshot_dir)` and calls `worldstate::tree_report(&facts)`, filling `findings.tree_states` and `findings.tree_ungradable` — "Which working trees these facts saw, and in how many states. Read from the same shipped `facts.jsonl`; nothing derived is stored, and a re-run recomputes it." So the authoring side's tree states ARE recoverable from artifacts shipped beside the memo.

note: src/worldstate.rs lines 78-100 (module doc, "Implementation choice") and line 167-170. A world-state marker is `git:<sha256 of "rev-parse HEAD" NUL "git diff HEAD --binary">` — "which together determine every tracked file's content: `HEAD` names the base, the diff names the delta from it". It was chosen over a worktree id precisely because a worktree id "only distinguishes *which* checkout you're in, not whether it's dirty — and the defect this fixes is exactly two facts taken against the same nominal checkout with opposite uncommitted content." Untracked files are excluded. Consequence carried by this definition: the marker changes on every commit and on any uncommitted edit to any tracked file, so a state observed in the past cannot be re-observed by a later pass unless that pass restores both HEAD and the exact working-tree delta.
